text:
With a planned capacity of 50,000 tonnes per year, the facility—whose location in France is currently being selected—is scheduled to start operations in 2030.

The ERA project further reinforces Axens’ industrial commitment to the transition toward low-carbon mobility, alongside the NACRE project – an advanced bioethanol production at the Lacq site, which has obtained its construction permit – and the MACARON project – a battery materials production in Valenciennes, which has recently submitted its construction permit application.

Industrial milestone for French SAF industry

The growing demand for SAF from the aviation sector requires expanding production beyond current SAF pathways based on used cooking oils (UCO) and animal fats (the so-called HEFA route).

The ERA project will help meet this need by broadening access to new SAF sources derived from biomass residues, representing an important step toward strengthening the energy sovereignty of French and European air transport.

Currently in the engineering phase, the project will be carried out by a dedicated project company named SAFIRIS and is targeted to begin production in 2030.

It will leverage the Jetanol technology developed by Axens and IFPEN, which has been proven in various petrochemical applications and optimized to maximize SAF yields.

The facility’s capacity has been set at 50,000 tonnes per year of SAF production, using advanced ethanol sourced from European feedstocks.

An industrial response to a sovereignty challenge

France set SAF blending targets as early as 2020, and Europe subsequently reinforced and expanded this ambition through the ReFuelEU Aviation regulation. For flights departing from France, this translates into over 1 million tonnes of SAF per annum by 2035.

Such a target represents a significant opportunity to develop French and European SAF production value chains based on domestic resources and technologies, complementing existing SAF production from UCO and animal fats, as well as future e-SAF production.

With its broad portfolio of SAF production technologies developed in partnership with IFPEN, covering all major production pathways — HEFA (oils and fats), advanced biofuels (ethanol and lignocellulosic biomass), e-SAF (hydrogen and carbon dioxide), and now methanol-based pathways through the acquisition of Air Liquide’s Methanol-to-Olefins technology — Axens has established itself as a leading technology and industrial player in the SAF sector.

With ERA, we are leveraging the full breadth of our technological expertise and project management capabilities to build, in France, an industrial sustainable aviation fuel value chain based on French and European resources. This is a sovereignty project as much as it is an energy transition project, bringing together the agricultural and low-carbon chemicals ecosystems. ERA, which will demonstrate the superior performance of our Jetanol technology, will serve as a replicable model for France, Europe and the rest of the world, said Quentin Debuisschert, CEO of Axens.

text:
Turkish Airlines, the airline that flies to more countries than any other airline, has signed an agreement to participate in the SAFFA Fund, a landmark investment fund aimed at accelerating the global production and deployment of sustainable aviation fuel (SAF).

In the long-term, the move will help reduce the environmental impact of South African travellers across the Turkish Airlines global network, aligning with the airline’s broader vision for sustainability, long-term growth, and supply-chain security.

The SAFFA Fund was launched in 2023 to increase the production capacity of sustainable aviation fuels and support the carbon-reduction targets of the global aviation sector. Investing in SAF projects that have reached technological maturity, the fund aims to build a diversified portfolio structure across different production technologies and geographic regions. The SAFFA Fund is managed by Burnham Sterling Asset Management (BSAM), with Airbus serving as the anchor investor alongside leading airlines and prominent global financial institutions.

Turkish Airlines’ participation in the fund secures access to sustainable aviation fuels while positioning Türkiye’s national flag carrier at the heart of technological innovation, investment, and feedstock development shaping the sector’s future. The partnership also deepens Turkish Airlines’ shared sustainability objectives with aircraft manufacturer Airbus.

Levent Konukcu, Chief Investment & Strategy Officer at Turkish Airlines, commented:

“With this investment in the SAFFA Fund, we aim not only to contribute to the development of the sustainable aviation fuel ecosystem, but also to maintain our active role in supporting innovative projects that shape the future of the industry. The strong international collaborations established through the SAFFA Fund will enable us to reinforce our supply security and contribute to the transformation of the global aviation sector, while supporting our access to sustainable aviation fuels.”

Michael Dickey Morgan, Executive Managing Director of Burnham Sterling Asset Management LLC, added:

“SAFFA Fund was built to channel capital into SAF projects across a mix of investments and geographies. Turkish Airlines’ investment adds scale to that strategy and evidences the confidence the Fund’s participants have in this asset class. Turkish Airlines’ commitment to the SAFFA Fund is a strong signal that the world’s leading carriers see this transition as essential for the long term. We’re proud to help drive that progress forward.”

Turkish Airlines will continue to drive the industry’s transformation through strategic partnerships and targeted investments that contribute to the widespread adoption of sustainable aviation fuels globally.

text: Sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) prices in Northwest Europe have risen 31% since the start of the Iran conflict. While geopolitical tensions helped drive the initial spike, BloombergNEF expects prices to remain elevated over the next year, averaging around $2,746 per metric ton. What's keeping prices high? Feedstocks. Feedstocks account for 70-80% of the cost of producing HEFA-SAF, and their prices are rising as road biofuel demand grows. New policies introduced in the EU and US in 2026 have boosted demand for renewable diesel and biodiesel, increasing competition for both feedstocks and, in some cases, production capacity. European SAF prices softened in early 2026, but this likely reflects seasonal buying patterns, with compliance-driven purchasing typically concentrated in the second half of the year. text:
India’s Ministry of Civil Aviation has reviewed national preparedness for the adoption of sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) and compliance with the International Civil Aviation Organization’s Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation (CORSIA). The high-level meeting, chaired by Civil Aviation Minister Ram Mohan Naidu on 29 July 2026, focused on SAF production, blending plans, carbon accounting systems and coordination across government agencies and industry stakeholders ahead of the mandatory phase of CORSIA beginning on 1 January 2027. Details of the meeting were published through the official government release.

Government reviews SAF supply and compliance planning

The meeting included representatives from the Ministry of Civil Aviation, Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas, Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change, the Directorate General of Civil Aviation, Airports Authority of India, Bureau of Indian Standards, Bureau of Energy Efficiency, airlines, airport operators and oil marketing companies.

Participants reviewed progress on SAF production facilities, certification systems and supply-chain development across the country. Discussions also examined timelines for bringing SAF production projects into operation and measures needed to meet anticipated demand from 2027 onwards.

The review forms part of broader efforts to strengthen India’s aviation systems and sustainability initiatives, alongside programmes such as safe helicopter operations management and wider digital modernisation initiatives across government.

Minister outlines transition from planning to implementation

“India is committed to building a robust and globally competitive sustainable aviation fuel ecosystem that supports the growth of our aviation sector while also contributing meaningfully to global carbon reduction efforts. Under the guidance of Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s vision of ‘One Earth, One Family, One Future’, we see SAF not merely as a compliance requirement, but as a strategic national opportunity.” Ram Mohan Naidu, Civil Aviation Minister, Government of India

The minister said the aviation sector had already undertaken several measures to reduce emissions, including the use of green energy at airports and support for modern fuel-efficient aircraft through leasing arrangements. According to the ministry, 104 airports in India currently operate using 100% green energy.

Naidu said the next stage would require movement from feasibility studies to firm production timelines, alongside clearly defined responsibilities for all stakeholders involved in production, distribution and accounting systems.

“Our immediate priority is to achieve the 1% CORSIA blending requirement in the most cost-effective way. As part of our long-term strategy, the carbon-credit adjustment mechanism should be developed through a whole-of-government approach.” Ram Mohan Naidu, Civil Aviation Minister, Government of India

National registry and accounting framework under discussion

The meeting also examined proposals for a national SAF registry capable of tracking fuel through the supply chain and supporting certification and market access requirements. Officials discussed the establishment of accounting, monitoring and reporting systems aligned with ICAO and CORSIA standards.

India is also considering mechanisms linked to carbon-credit adjustments and the development of a domestic CORSIA-compliant carbon market framework. According to the ministry, these measures are intended to support both emissions reduction and the long-term competitiveness of India’s aviation sector.

The discussions reflected the increasing use of coordinated digital systems and data-driven governance in public administration, similar to projects such as the NeVA digital legislative programme and other technology-led government initiatives.

Draft SAF policy approaches final stage

Naidu confirmed that India’s draft SAF policy is in its final stages following a series of inter-ministerial consultations and stakeholder discussions. He said the government aimed to minimise the financial burden on both passengers and airlines while identifying cost-efficient production and distribution mechanisms.

“We need to ensure that this process places the minimum possible burden on passengers and airlines. For this, we must study all possible SAF pathways and identify the most cost-efficient mechanisms, from production to airport delivery.” Ram Mohan Naidu, Civil Aviation Minister, Government of India

The ministry stated that coordinated implementation across government bodies and industry participants would be essential to ensure readiness before the mandatory CORSIA phase begins in January 2027. The government also reiterated its commitment to increasing domestic SAF production, strengthening aviation infrastructure and reducing carbon emissions from international aviation.

Sources: Delta Air Lines, “Delta Joins Minnesota Leaders to Celebrate Opening of New SAF Blending Facility Serving MSP,” July 27, 2026; Minnesota Sustainable Aviation Fuel Hub; KARE 11, report on the Pine Bend sustainable aviation fuel facility
text:
ROSEMOUNT, MN (July 30, 2026). Minnesota officials and aviation industry leaders have marked the completion of a sustainable aviation fuel blending facility intended to expand the supply of lower-carbon fuel available to airlines at Minneapolis-St. Paul International Airport.

The facility is located at Flint Hills Resources’ Pine Bend refinery in Rosemount. It can receive, store and blend as much as 30 million gallons of unblended sustainable aviation fuel annually, according to Delta Air Lines and the Minnesota Sustainable Aviation Fuel Hub.

The project connects the blended fuel to MSP Airport through existing pipeline infrastructure.

Despite some reports describing the development as a production facility, the Rosemount operation does not manufacture the sustainable aviation fuel. It receives what the industry calls “neat” sustainable aviation fuel, blends it with conventional jet fuel and delivers the resulting product for use by aircraft at MSP.

That distinction matters when evaluating the project’s size, economic effect and environmental benefit.

Sustainable aviation fuel can be made from feedstocks including used cooking oil, agricultural products, animal fats and other renewable or waste-derived materials. The source, manufacturing method and transportation distance can significantly affect the fuel’s overall greenhouse-gas performance.

The alternative fuel must currently be blended with conventional jet fuel before it can be used in commercial aircraft under existing technical standards.

Delta joined state officials, Minnesota Sustainable Aviation Fuel Hub members and other partners July 27 to celebrate the facility’s completion. MSP is Delta’s second-largest hub, making the airport a significant location for efforts to increase commercial use of alternative aviation fuels.

Delta says it uses approximately 250 million gallons of jet fuel annually at MSP. The blending facility’s maximum annual capacity of 30 million gallons of unblended sustainable aviation fuel would represent a portion of that demand rather than a complete replacement for petroleum-based jet fuel.

The airline has set a goal of having sustainable aviation fuel account for 10 percent of its fuel use across its network by 2030.

Supporters say the Rosemount facility addresses an infrastructure problem that has limited wider adoption. Airlines need a reliable system for receiving, testing, storing, blending and delivering alternative fuel in commercial quantities. Pine Bend already has large storage tanks, rail-unloading capacity, laboratories, filtration systems and pipeline connections to the airport.

The project is part of the Minnesota Sustainable Aviation Fuel Hub, a coalition of airlines, businesses, agricultural interests, government bodies, universities and nonprofit organizations working to build a regional supply chain.

Minnesota officials say the emerging industry could create new markets for farmers and support jobs connected to fuel processing, transportation and aviation. Those economic outcomes will depend on where the fuel is produced, which feedstocks are used and whether regional production grows alongside blending and distribution capacity.

Sustainable aviation fuel is generally promoted as a way to reduce life-cycle greenhouse-gas emissions compared with conventional jet fuel. It does not eliminate emissions from aircraft engines, and the precise reduction varies according to the feedstock and production process.

The completed Rosemount facility provides MSP with infrastructure to use the fuel at a larger commercial scale. Its environmental significance will ultimately depend on how much sustainable fuel passes through the facility, how that fuel is produced and how consistently airlines replace conventional jet fuel with qualifying alternatives.

title: Air Canada and Airbus to invest in sustainable aviation fuel development in Canada
description:
Air Canada and Airbus have announced plans to establish a joint investment platform aimed at supporting the development of commercial-scale sustainable aviation fuel production in Canada.
The cooperation is intended to accelerate the development of at least one Canadian sustainable aviation fuel project toward a final investment decision.
Kitcher said Canada has considerable potential in terms of the feedstocks required for sustainable aviation fuel production.
As part of its first allocation, Airbus will purchase verified environmental attributes associated with more than 60,000 litres of sustainable aviation fuel.
Sustainable aviation fuel is an umbrella term for a family of alternative synthetic fuels produced from renewable feedstocks.
text:
Air Canada and Airbus have announced plans to establish a joint investment platform aimed at supporting the development of commercial-scale sustainable aviation fuel production in Canada. Through the platform, the two companies intend to invest up to approximately CAD 13.7 million, equivalent to US$10 million, in projects related to SAF production.

The cooperation is intended to accelerate the development of at least one Canadian sustainable aviation fuel project toward a final investment decision. Air Canada and Airbus emphasise that an appropriate regulatory framework and support from federal and provincial authorities will also be necessary to establish a competitive domestic market.

The companies are also working with the Canadian Council for Sustainable Aviation Fuels, C-SAF, to align private investment, public policy and the development of domestic production capacity. The ultimate objective is to improve the availability of renewable fuels for Canada’s aviation sector while maintaining the affordability of air travel.

Air Canada Vice President of Airport Affairs, Corporate Real Estate and Sustainability Valerie Durand said the joint initiative with Airbus represents an important step in the energy transition of Canadian aviation.

According to Durand, the project should support domestic SAF production, help corporate customers address emissions associated with business travel and contribute to a long-term reduction in the aviation industry’s carbon footprint.

Airbus Chief Sustainability Officer and Communications Julie Kitcher stressed that aviation decarbonisation will require long-term cooperation across the industry, as well as significant investment in new renewable energy sources.

Kitcher said Canada has considerable potential in terms of the feedstocks required for sustainable aviation fuel production. Combined with suitable public policies, the development of such an industry could contribute to emissions reductions, economic growth and job creation.

Alongside the joint investment platform, Airbus has also signed a five-year agreement to participate in Air Canada’s Leave Less Travel programme. The programme is designed for corporate customers seeking to support the use of SAF and reduce emissions associated with business travel.

As part of its first allocation, Airbus will purchase verified environmental attributes associated with more than 60,000 litres of sustainable aviation fuel. Air Canada will track greenhouse gas emissions generated by business travel undertaken by Airbus employees and retire the corresponding environmental attributes on the company’s behalf.

Such mechanisms do not necessarily mean that SAF is physically supplied to the aircraft used by a particular passenger. Instead, they allow companies to finance its use within the wider fuel supply system. Corporate customers thereby stimulate demand and market development, while the associated emissions reductions are recorded through a certified accounting system.

Air Canada is also linking SAF development with the modernisation of its fleet. The Canadian carrier is introducing more efficient aircraft, including the Airbus A321XLR and the Canada-built Airbus A220. These aircraft consume less fuel than the models they replace, while SAF could further reduce their life-cycle emissions.

Air Canada and Airbus support the aviation industry’s ambition to achieve net-zero carbon emissions by 2050. Sustainable aviation fuel is regarded as one of the most important tools for reaching that target, particularly because it can be used in existing aircraft and fuel supply systems with limited technical modifications.

Airbus and consulting firm ICF have also published a macroeconomic study indicating that Canada has significant potential to develop an aviation biofuels industry.

According to the study, producing enough SAF to cover 40% of Canada’s aviation fuel demand by 2040 could add CAD 32 billion to the country’s gross domestic product and support the creation of approximately 140,000 jobs.

The economic benefits could be distributed across agricultural, forestry and urban regions, depending on the types of feedstocks used, the production processes selected and the locations of future facilities.

Sustainable aviation fuel is an umbrella term for a family of alternative synthetic fuels produced from renewable feedstocks. It is chemically similar to conventional jet fuel, but is made from non-fossil sources and can therefore deliver lower greenhouse gas emissions over its full life cycle.

The announced cooperation between Air Canada and Airbus is intended to address both supply and demand. The investment platform is focused on developing production capacity, while the Leave Less Travel programme is expected to increase corporate demand for SAF and its associated environmental attributes.

However, the project’s full potential will depend on regulatory support, feedstock availability, production costs and the industry’s ability to narrow the price gap between sustainable and conventional aviation fuel.

title: US-Saudi consortium advances $5-billion GCC refining, export hub project
description:
After 3 years of evaluating locations across the Mideast Gulf, the consortium said it has narrowed site discussions to three GCC locations outside the Strait of Hormuz.
Further details regarding the shortlist and a specific deadline for non-shortlisted GCC members to respond with alternative proposals were not revealed.
Once a host jurisdiction is confirmed, the partners said the project would move into final site diligence and engineering design.
The consortium also confirmed discussions are underway with feedstock providers within and beyond the GCC, with definitive arrangements anticipated to progress in parallel with the final host selection.
The consortium confirmed it is also evaluating sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) co-processing and carbon-management capabilities as potential future components of the planned development.
text:
MWG Enterprises LLC, Patel Family Office (PTO), and Saudi Arabia-based AHQ Group’s Pipe & Well Services Co. (PWS) have formed a private US-Saudi consortium that aims to build a new integrated refining complex and associated port located within a yet-to-be-determined country of the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC), members of which include the United Arab Emirates (UAE), Bahrain, Saudi Arabia, Oman, Qatar, and Kuwait.

The consortium—officially named MERA Oil—has entered the final stage of host-site selection for the planned $5-billion integrated refinery and energy export corridor, which, if completed, will have crude oil processing capacity of 200,000 b/d, the sponsors and MGW Enterprises said in separate July 29 releases.

After 3 years of evaluating locations across the Mideast Gulf, the consortium said it has narrowed site discussions to three GCC locations outside the Strait of Hormuz.

Following talks progressing during the past 2 years specifically with the shortlisted jurisdictions, MERA Oil is approaching a decision point, with official selection of a definitive host location likely to be confirmed by yearend 2026, according to the partners.

Despite the shortlist, the consortium said it continues to remain open to a “decisively superior” proposition from another qualifying GCC jurisdiction that can meet route-resilience, infrastructure, and development timing requirements before making its final selection.

Further details regarding the shortlist and a specific deadline for non-shortlisted GCC members to respond with alternative proposals were not revealed.

Project scope, infrastructure concept

Phase 1 of the planned MERA Oil development would include the 200,000-b/d integrated refinery linked to deepwater port infrastructure, as well as large-scale storage installations for crude oil and refined products, the consortium said.

The project’s marine export operations would be designed to provide direct access to international shipping routes while remaining outside embattled Strait of Hormuz.

The consortium said the planned integrated complex and port operations—which would have a targeted 100-year project lifetime—intends to support an industrial base for refining, storage, logistics, technical capability, and energy security in the region

Project status, timeline

To date, the sponsors said a pre-feasibility study covering refinery configuration, product slate, preliminary capital requirements, logistics, and phased execution has reached an advanced stage.

Once a host jurisdiction is confirmed, the partners said the project would move into final site diligence and engineering design.

If approved, Phase 1 of the project is slated to reach mechanical completion by yearend 2029, followed by commissioning and commercial operations.

The consortium also confirmed discussions are underway with feedstock providers within and beyond the GCC, with definitive arrangements anticipated to progress in parallel with the final host selection.

Product slate, emissions controls

The refinery’s proposed product slate would focus on high-quality middle distillates, including ultralow-sulfur diesel and jet fuel destined to import-dependent markets in the US, the Atlantic Basin, the Mideast Gulf region, and other international markets, subject to final engineering and offtake arrangements, the consortium said.

According to the partners, Phase 1 is intended to incorporate unspecified energy-efficient refining technologies and advanced emissions-control systems.

The consortium confirmed it is also evaluating sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) co-processing and carbon-management capabilities as potential future components of the planned development.

Investment structure, employment

The consortium said it expects the $5-billion Phase 1 capital program—financing structures of which would be compliant with Islam’s Shariah religious and moral legal framework— to draw on sponsor equity, sovereign and institutional participation, international project finance, and export-credit support.

For the selected host jurisdiction, the sponsors said that, based on preliminary estimates, the project—which would require 1,200-1,500 acres of port-connected industrial land—could support up to 3,000 direct jobs at peak during construction, commissioning, and operations, along with up to 15,000 indirect employment opportunities.

title: Why retail warehouse leaders still can't scale their technology - SmartBrief
description:
It is a fundamental misunderstanding of how retail warehouse technology should scale, and that misunderstanding is costing retailers more than most realize.
Why the ladder mindset fails For decades, retail warehouse technology has followed a maturity-level model, which practitioners often call a ladder.
It sounds logical, but it has a structural flaw: it treats the technology platform as temporary rather than as a permanent foundation.
What technology leaders should be asking For retail leaders evaluating a WMS, the most useful questions aren’t about feature lists.
Leaders’ frustration with implementing retail warehouse technology starts with how the industry has framed maturity.
text:
Retail supply chain and warehouse leaders keep running into the same wall. A retailer grows, adds a distribution or fulfillment center, or expands into a new market, and quickly finds that its warehouse management system was never built to keep pace.

What follows is a disruptive, expensive reimplementation cycle that strains IT teams and forces warehouse employees to relearn systems from scratch. For many retailers, this is not a one-time event. It is a recurring cost of doing business in a sector where technology decisions compound, especially as store, ecommerce and marketplace fulfillment all draw on the same network.

The root cause is not a shortage of technology options. It is a fundamental misunderstanding of how retail warehouse technology should scale, and that misunderstanding is costing retailers more than most realize.

Why the ladder mindset fails

For decades, retail warehouse technology has followed a maturity-level model, which practitioners often call a ladder. Retailers at a smaller scale start with a basic platform, and as order volume grows, conventional wisdom holds that they must upgrade to a more sophisticated platform. It sounds logical, but it has a structural flaw: it treats the technology platform as temporary rather than as a permanent foundation.

The ladder model drives the cycle of costly reimplementation. When a retailer outgrows its system, it does not simply add capability. It replaces the platform entirely, along with new training, new integrations with ecommerce and order management tools and new project risk. Major WMS vendors reinforce this by offering tiered product lines, lighter versions for smaller fulfillment centers and more robust versions for complex, omnichannel operations. In practice, the lighter versions are often the same software with features stripped out. When retailers need capabilities like ship-from-store or same-day fulfillment, they find they cannot upgrade within a platform. They are switching platforms entirely.

The hidden cost of patchwork architecture

The ladder approach creates a second, less visible problem: fragmented operational intelligence. As retailers expand across multiple fulfillment centers, they often accumulate different WMS platforms through acquisitions, regional rollouts, or phased implementations.

Each system may work well on its own, but they rarely measure KPIs the same way. Metrics such as order accuracy, units picked per hour, cycle time and on-time-ship performance are often defined differently across systems, leading to inconsistent network-wide reporting.

Retail leaders end up reconciling spreadsheets and making decisions without a unified view of network performance, which slows decision-making and buries opportunities to improve fulfillment across the retail enterprise.

Configuration over customization: A better framework

A growing number of retail operations leaders are rethinking the ladder model in favor of what might be called a dial approach. Instead of picking a platform sized for today’s scale and swapping it out later, the dial model treats the WMS as a permanent foundation. Capability isn’t added by switching platforms. It’s activated within the same platform as the business and its fulfillment channels evolve.

The key distinction is customization versus configuration. Traditional WMS rollouts often require custom code to handle retail-specific processes like order routing or store-replenishment logic. Custom code diverges from the base system, so every release becomes a risk, and maintaining that code gets more expensive over time.

Configuration-based systems let retailers adjust behavior through logic rules and decision tables instead of code. If a distribution center doesn’t need each-pick replenishment because it ships full cases, that capability simply isn’t turned on. It’s still there if the retailer later adds an ecommerce channel, with no technical debt in the meantime. Software updates don’t require reconciling custom code, so upgrades stay routine and implementation timelines stay short. Operations change, but create no technical debt in the meantime. When a software update is released, there is no custom code to reconcile. Implementation timelines shorten. Upgrades become routine. And when an operation evolves, the same platform accommodates the change through configuration rather than replacement.

Multisite consistency without multiplatform complexity

The dial model shows up clearly in configuration templates deployed across a retail network. Rather than building each site’s setup from scratch, retailers can define templates by facility type and roll them out as the network grows. A store-replenishment center gets one template, a highly automated fulfillment center gets another, and both run on the same platform.

Training stays consistent because the underlying system doesn’t change. Integration work with ecommerce and carrier systems is done once and applies everywhere. And as a facility’s operations become more complex, the same system grows with it by enabling new capabilities rather than triggering a replacement project. Integration work done once applies everywhere.

And when a facility grows from a simpler operational model to a more complex one, the system grows with it by activating additional capabilities rather than triggering a replacement project.

What technology leaders should be asking

For retail leaders evaluating a WMS, the most useful questions aren’t about feature lists. Feature parity across major vendors is high; the questions that matter now are architectural.

Does the platform need custom code for retail-specific processes, or can it adapt through configuration? Will a future upgrade break those configurations? Can the same platform run a small store-replenishment center and a large, automated omnichannel fulfillment center without switching products? And is the vendor’s road map built to make retailers outgrow the current product, the way tiered lines often do, or to keep evolving alongside them?

The answers show whether a retailer is buying a ladder or a dial. When operational agility is a competitive requirement and reimplementation costs keep compounding, that distinction outweighs any single feature comparison.

Leaders’ frustration with implementing retail warehouse technology starts with how the industry has framed maturity. Moving from a ladder model to a dial model doesn’t just cut costs. It changes what a retailer can do operationally and how fast it can respond when the business needs something new.

text:
Zurich, July 29, 2026

Synhelion has been selected for funding under the “Produktives.NRW” program of the German state of North Rhine-Westphalia (NRW), supporting the construction of a commercial demonstration plant for renewable synthetic fuels at Brainergy Park in Jülich, Germany. The program draws on around EUR 90 million in EU funding from the Just Transition Fund, which is being distributed across nine selected projects supporting industrial innovation in the Rhenish region and the northern Ruhr area.

Synhelion’s synthetic fuel plant is one of nine projects with market-ready solutions for sustainable key technologies selected in the fourth round of the Produktives.NRW funding program.

The selection supports Synhelion’s next scale-up step. The company plans to build a commercial demonstration plant in Jülich, Germany, building on the successful operation of its first plant, DAWN, and further scaling its fuel production technology. While plant DAWN de-risked and validated Synhelion’s technology at industrial scale, the next plant will establish commercial operability and make the technology bankable. The majority of the plant’s output is already covered by binding long-term offtake agreements with major customers.

“Being selected under the Produktives.NRW program is a strong endorsement of our technology and commercialization strategy, and we are grateful to the state of North Rhine-Westphalia for supporting our project. By building our next plant in Jülich, we are strengthening Germany as an industrial location for renewable synthetic fuels and contributing to a more resilient, diversified, and less import-dependent energy supply in Europe,” says Philipp Furler, Co-CEO and Co-Founder of Synhelion.

Renewable fuels made in Germany

Synhelion produces renewable synthetic fuels that can directly replace fossil fuels without requiring changes to existing engines or fuel infrastructure. Its portfolio includes sustainable aviation fuel (SAF), renewable synthetic diesel, and renewable synthetic gasoline. The fuels reduce net CO₂ emissions by up to 100% compared with fossil fuels and are aimed at sectors that are difficult to electrify, such as aviation and long-distance transportation. The planned commercial demonstration plant in Jülich will represent the next milestone in scaling Synhelion’s technology from industrial demonstration to commercial production.

Supporting industrial innovation in North Rhine-Westphalia

The Produktives.NRW program implements the European Union’s Strategic Technologies for Europe Platform (STEP) in NRW. It aims to reduce strategic dependencies, promote the development of technologies made in Europe, and strengthen the competitiveness and resilience of industry.

The program is part of the EFRE/JTF NRW 2021–2027 framework and supports strategic projects that strengthen innovation, competitiveness, and the transition toward a more sustainable economy. It is jointly run by NRW’s Ministry of Economic Affairs, Industry, Climate Action and Energy and its Ministry of the Environment, Nature and Transport. By supporting Synhelion’s technology, NRW recognizes the potential of locally produced synthetic fuels to support transport defossilization and energy security.

text:
Union Civil Aviation Minister Ram Mohan Naidu reviews India's preparedness for SAF and CORSIA implementation

New Delhi, July 30

The meeting was attended by Secretary (Civil Aviation) and senior officials from the Ministry of Civil Aviation, Ministry of Petroleum & Natural Gas, Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change, Directorate General of Civil Aviation (DGCA), Airports Authority of India (AAI), Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS), Bureau of Energy Efficiency (BEE), Oil Marketing Companies (OMCs), airlines, airport operators and other key stakeholders.

According to the release, "The meeting reviewed the progress made in SAF production, certification, and supply chain development across the country. The status of various SAF production projects being implemented by Oil Marketing Companies and the timelines for commissioning these facilities were also reviewed. Stakeholders deliberated on measures required to ensure the timely availability of Sustainable Aviation Fuel to meet the anticipated demand from 2027 onwards."

Speaking on the occasion, Minister for Civil Aviation Ram Mohan Naidu said, "India is committed to building a robust and globally competitive Sustainable Aviation Fuel ecosystem that supports the growth of our aviation sector while contributing meaningfully to global decarbonisation efforts. Guided by Prime Minister Narendra Modi's vision of 'One Earth, One Family, One Future', we are approaching SAF not merely as a compliance requirement but as a strategic national opportunity. Multiple stakeholders, including the farmers, stand to gain from the SAF value chain."

The Minister further stated, "As an industry, we are already working on multiple fronts to reduce emissions. From 0 in 2014, today 104 airports in the country have switched entirely to 100% green energy usage. By encouraging the leasing ecosystem, airlines are being supported to have modern and fuel-efficient fleets. SAF is also a critical component for our collective efforts. We must now move from feasibility studies to concrete production timelines and from ambition to action. Every stakeholder needs to have clear obligations for ensuring adequate production as well as robust accounting. Our immediate priority is to achieve the 1% CORSIA blending requirement in the most cost-effective manner. As part of our long-term strategy, the carbon-credit offset mechanism must be developed through a whole-of-government approach."

Ram Mohan Naidu reviewed the proposed implementation roadmap for the SAF blending mandate, including the roles and responsibilities of Oil Marketing Companies, airlines and airport operators. Discussions were held on establishing a robust accounting, monitoring and reporting framework aligned with ICAO/CORSIA requirements, development of a national SAF Registry with end-to-end traceability and measures to facilitate certification and market access.

Emphasising the importance of coordinated execution, the Minister said, "This transition must be driven through collective decision-making and close coordination among all stakeholders. We reviewed progress in SAF supply-chain development, the national SAF Registry, accounting and reporting systems and measures required for effective CORSIA compliance. I am encouraged by the significant progress already made and by the commitment shown by all participating Ministries and industry stakeholders. We have directed all concerned stakeholders to expedite the identified action points so that India is fully prepared well before the mandatory phase of CORSIA begins on 1 January 2027."

Talking about the SAF Policy and the financial impact of SAF, the Minister added, "The draft SAF policy is now in its final stages. So, we are doing multiple such inter-ministerial consultations and stakeholder engagements at various levels. For me voice of the passenger remains central and passenger happen to be the most important stakeholder of our industry. We have to ensure that this process imposes the least possible burden on passengers and airlines. For that we need to study all the possible SAF pathways and within pathways identify the most cost-effective mechanism right from production to drop-in at the airport."

The meeting further deliberated on India's preparedness for CORSIA implementation, including the issuance of Letters of Authorisation and the development of a CORSIA-compliant carbon market framework in India.

"The Government of India remains committed to promoting domestic production of Sustainable Aviation Fuel, strengthening India's aviation ecosystem, reducing carbon emissions from international aviation and positioning India as a global leader in sustainable aviation," the release said.

Roeslein Renewables seeks to tap demand through marine biofuel, which it says could dwarf sustainable aviation fuel.

Biogas and livestock producers could see gains from a UN vote on a maritime emissions framework, Roeslein says.

Final 45Z tax credit rules could unleash hundreds of millions of dollars in biogas investment, industry group says.

Biogas — created with organic raw materials like livestock manure and leftover corn cobs — is having a moment.

As agriculture focuses on reliable domestic fertilizer supplies, circular economies, and renewable marine fuel, enthusiasts say the biogas industry checks all these boxes and more.

A challenge, though, is describing the scope of what the business entails, says Bryan Sievers, an Iowa farmer and director of government relations for St. Louis-based Roeslein Renewables, which designs, builds and operates renewable natural gas (RNG) facilities.

“It’s not cookie-cutter,” says Sievers, who serves on the board of the American Biogas Council. “It's not like doing a solar farm or wind installation. Every project we do is unique and different.”

The biogas industry converts manure, wastewater, food waste, crop residues such as corn stover, and captured landfill gas into RNG, renewable electricity, heat and natural fertilizer. Industry-wide biogas capture capacity climbed about 8% in 2025, according to the American Biogas Council.

Roeslein partners with dairy farmers and others to create RNG from farm waste and wild plants like prairie grasses, and cover crops. A byproduct of the process is nutrient-heavy digestate that can be used as barn bedding for dairy cows and sustainable fertilizer. “You're producing your own fertilizer for your own crops, and in a form that's easy to apply,” Sievers tells Agri-Pulse. “You don’t care if there's nitrogen tied up on a ship in the Strait of Hormuz — you’re independent.”

The digestate, or treated manure that’s 99% free of pathogens, is created through Roeslein’s anaerobic digester systems that produce RNG for fueling vehicles and other modes of transportation, among other uses. The digestate leftover is usable in solid or liquid form and can be stored until a crop grower is ready to apply it. Typically, the material is applied in the fall after harvest, or in the spring prior to planting. There are no shelf-life limitations for digestate.

“What we're doing in that 45-day window is what it takes nature somewhere between three and five years to break down residue in the field,” Sievers says. “It’s basically a big ruminant stomach you're doing this in, in the digester, and putting it back out in the field when it's time.”

45Z outlook

The biogas industry represents $40 billion in deployed capital across all U.S. states, the council says. There are also “hundreds of millions of dollars” in investment available for transforming organic waste into domestic energy and fertilizer, but the money is on hold until final 45Z Clean Fuel Production Tax Credit rules are out from the Treasury Department, according to the group.

The credit, which originated in the Biden era and was then picked up and revamped by the Trump administration and Congress, is valued based on the lifecycle greenhouse gas emission of a fuel’s production, with lower “carbon intensity” scores getting premiums. While the industry is still awaiting final details, overall, this means fuel made from waste products is highly prized.

Biogas projects capture methane — a vastly more powerful greenhouse gas than carbon dioxide — that would otherwise be spewed into the atmosphere. That means biogas can have a carbon intensity 50% to 700% lower than fossil fuels, the council says.

Yet once 45Z regulations are final, the next big challenge is around the corner. The credit currently is set to expire at the end of 2029. “It's a very short runway,” Sievers says.

One idea being kicked around is advocating for 45Z-type incentives at the state level, especially in the farm-heavy Midwest, according to Sievers.

Meanwhile, RNG accounted for 94% of all on-road fuel used in U.S. natural gas vehicles last year, as opposed to the fossil counterpart, with use nearly doubling since 2021, according to the Transport Project.

The success is prompting Roeslein, and the RNG and biofuel industries overall, to look toward the seas for new growth opportunities.

Marine fuel push

Roeslein is a member of the American Biofuels Maritime Initiative, which aims to work with the Trump administration and Congress to craft policies to speed up use of American-made energy and biofuels in the global maritime industry. The goal is to secure U.S. dominance in international maritime shipping.

The group was formed last December by the American Biogas Council and the Renewable Fuels Association, a major ethanol trade group. Other members include the National Corn Growers Association, Clean Fuels Alliance America, Growth Energy and Marquis.

“We’re looking at the maritime industry as a way to build new demand for all biofuels,” Sievers says, adding that the united approach also doesn't hurt in getting the attention of policymakers. “We’re hitting it out of the park,” he adds, referring to outreach efforts.

The USDA in general is both "enthusiastic and proactive" about international maritime as the "largest market opportunity for farmers and livestock producers," Sievers says, adding that the Office of the Chief Economist, Foreign Ag Service, Undersecretary for Trade and Foreign Agricultual Affairs Luke Lindberg and political advisers "are all buzzing about international maritime demand opportunities for biofuels."

Global marine policy will be in the forefront later this year as the UN’s International Maritime Organization considers a Net-Zero Framework, a proposed cap-and-trade-type system that would require ocean-going vessels to cut greenhouse gas emissions. Trump rejected it as a "global carbon tax," prompting IMO to delay its vote by a year.

Yet Roeslein, RFA and other U.S. biofuel and ag groups say a global framework could be a game-changer for U.S. biofuels, including ethanol, biodiesel, and a liquified form of renewable natural gas, known as bioLNG and produced from manure or landfill gas.

NCGA estimates up to 3 billion bushels a year in additional demand if ethanol adoption for maritime fuel grows to just 10% of the market. Sievers says there's a similar opportunity for soybeans through the use of biodiesel for ships.

On the biogas front, the U.S. recently submitted a paper to the IMO arguing that manure-based RNG should get credit for the methane gas it keeps out of the atmosphere when used as marine fuel. The paper notes that there’s already a precedent for programs that credit avoided methane for RNG, including in the U.S., California, Canada and the European Union.

"The outcome will help determine whether livestock manure digester gas can compete in the global marine fuel market taking shape under the IMO's Net-Zero Framework," Sophia Stone, Roeslein's assistant director for government relations, tells Agri-Pulse.

Overall, the bioLNG and biodiesel markets alone for maritime shipping could generate $100 billion to $200 billion in new U.S. farm revenues by 2050, according to Roeslein.

"The maritime fuel opportunity would answer the question of farmers wanting trade, not aid," Stone says. "They wouldn't really have to rely on subsidies. We're opening up new markets for farmers that would really dwarf sustainable aviation fuel."

text:
Canada now has a national roadmap to hit 10 percent sustainable aviation fuel use by 2030, about one billion litres a year (Transport Canada, 2026). Transport Canada's new Sustainable Aviation Fuels Blueprint lays out seven pillars of action to get there. British Columbia already shows the approach can work in practice.

The Blueprint was developed with Deloitte, the Sustainable Aviation Task Force, and the Canadian Council for Sustainable Aviation Fuels (C-SAF). C-SAF is a national organization of more than 60 airlines and industry members that co-led the report's development.

>> In Other News: Carbon To Sea Initiative Awards $225,000 To Study Ocean Alkalinity Enhancement In Wastewater Treatment

What Does Canada's New SAF Blueprint Actually Say?

The Blueprint sets out seven pillars of action to help Canada reach its aspirational goal of 10 percent SAF use by 2030 (Transport Canada, 2026). It builds on Canada's Aviation Climate Action Plan, first released in 2022.

The pillars target three core barriers to SAF growth. These barriers are high cost, investment risk, and limited global supply. Individual pillars cover strategic partnerships, de-risking investment, supply chains, codes and standards, technology development, emissions accounting, and public education.

SAF costs 2 to 8 times more than conventional jet fuel today (Transport Canada, 2026)

No commercial SAF production facility currently operates in Canada (Transport Canada, 2026)

Announced Canadian SAF projects already total more than one billion litres of potential yearly capacity (Transport Canada, 2026)

Canadian air carriers released 22 megatonnes of greenhouse gas emissions in 2023 (Transport Canada, 2026). That marks a 23 percent increase since 2005. The Blueprint frames SAF as the most commercially ready tool available today. It works as a drop-in replacement in existing aircraft engines, with no modifications needed.

>> RELATED: Boeing Backs $10M Quebec SAF Project to Fly by 2027

How Much Fuel Does the 10% Target Represent?

Canada's 10 percent goal equals roughly one billion litres of SAF used every year by 2030 (Transport Canada, 2026). Total Canadian jet fuel demand is projected to reach approximately 10.6 billion litres that same year, according to Canadian Energy Regulator estimates.

Canada's refineries already produced 6.4 billion litres of conventional jet fuel in 2024 (Statistics Canada, 2024). Much of that fuel serves the domestic market. Some is exported to the United States and China. The refining base already exists. What is missing is dedicated SAF production layered on top of it.

Global SAF output is growing fast, even from a small base. Production doubled year over year for three straight years (International Air Transport Association, 2024).

Year Global SAF Production (million litres) 2021 99.9 2022 300 2023 600 2024 1,300 2025 (projected) 2,700

Source: International Air Transport Association, 2024

Is British Columbia Proof That SAF Policy Works?

British Columbia's results suggest yes. Low carbon jet fuel reached 3.9 percent of the province's total jet fuel supply in 2025 (Government of British Columbia, 2026). That figure beat B.C.'s own volumetric requirement of 3 percent by 2030. The province hit the mark five years early. B.C.'s Low Carbon Fuel Standard has required lower carbon intensity in aviation fuel since 2026. A separate renewable content mandate is set to start at 1 percent in 2028, then rise to 3 percent by 2030.

Across all fuel categories, B.C.'s clean fuel rules avoided more than 5 million metric tons of greenhouse gas emissions in 2025 (Government of British Columbia, 2026). Cumulatively since 2010, the province has avoided over 32.7 million tons. Similar public-private coordination already underpins Canada's direct air capture protocol, one of the country's other major carbon management frameworks.

How Does Canada's Target Compare to the U.S. and U.K.?

Canada's 10 percent by 2030 goal sits in the middle of the pack globally. The United States is chasing 11.3 billion litres of domestic SAF production by 2030 under its SAF Grand Challenge. That target is backed by an estimated 44 billion U.S. dollars in announced investment.

The United Kingdom takes a different approach. Instead of an aspirational goal, it uses a binding supplier mandate. The mandate started at 2 percent in 2025. It rises on a straight line to 10 percent by 2030, then 22 percent by 2040.

Jurisdiction 2030 SAF Target Policy Type Canada 10% (about 1 billion litres) Aspirational goal United States 11.3 billion litres Incentive-driven target United Kingdom 10%, rising to 22% by 2040 Binding supplier mandate European Union 6%, rising to 70% by 2050 Binding blending mandate

What Projects Are Already Building Toward the Goal?

Several Canadian projects are moving ahead of the Blueprint's release. In Québec, Boeing is putting 10 million Canadian dollars into Project Avance, a sawmill-residue SAF facility. Production there is expected to start in 2027.

Ontario is backing a different feedstock path. The province committed 5.5 million Canadian dollars to a wood-based SAF demonstration plant in Thunder Bay. The project will use mill byproducts and underused wood fibre.

These regional projects sit under the national framework the Blueprint just formalized. Similar coordination has already scaled hydrogen hub development on the U.S. Gulf Coast. Canada's Blueprint draws on comparable public-private structures.

Carbon removal projects show the same government-industry model working nearby. Deep Sky's direct air capture deployment in Montreal is one example.

Momentum is building across North America too. Record U.S. SAF production volumes and on-airport SAF production in Pittsburgh both point the same direction. Even the recent retention of U.S. federal funding for hydrogen and carbon storage hubs signals durable policy support region-wide.

Official C-SAF video featuring Executive Director Geoff Tauvette explaining how sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) can cut aviation lifecycle emissions by up to 80% as a practical, drop-in solution to help Canada advance cleaner aviation.

The Runway Ahead

Canada's Blueprint does not pretend the path is easy. SAF still costs 2 to 8 times more than jet fuel. No Canadian facility has reached a final investment decision yet.

But the document gives industry something it lacked before. It offers a coordinated federal framework built with input from over 90 stakeholders across the aviation and fuels value chain. Combined with B.C.'s early results, Canada now has both a plan and proof that the plan can work.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Canada's 10 percent SAF target mandatory?

No. It remains an aspirational goal under the Aviation Climate Action Plan, not a binding federal mandate. British Columbia does have its own binding volumetric requirement at the provincial level.

Does Canada currently produce SAF commercially?

Not yet. As of 2025, there was no sustained commercial SAF production in Canada, though announced projects total more than one billion litres of potential annual capacity.

What feedstocks will Canadian SAF likely use?

Canola, forestry residues, used cooking oil, and agricultural waste are the leading candidates, given Canada's existing feedstock base and refining expertise.

text:
There’s some seriously good news for small businesses right now: Consumer love for independent brands is soaring.

However, as any business owner will tell you, a surge in interest brings a new set of challenges. With social media now serving as a primary way for consumers to discover brands, small business owners find themselves playing the role of content creators on top of every other hat they’ve got to wear.

In addition, they’re navigating an economy where buyers are more carefully evaluating every dollar they spend.

For Constant Contact’s Small Business Now report, we surveyed more than 5,000 small business owners and consumers across the US, UK, Canada, Australia and New Zealand to understand the current landscape.

We discovered that to stay visible while managing the daily hustle of running a business, small and medium-sized businesses are fundamentally rewriting their job descriptions to embrace the role of “creator” — and leaning on AI to get it all done.

Social media discovery means everyone’s a creator

It seems like everyone’s a creator these days, and it’s not just because they want to be social media stars. It comes down to how today’s consumers shop.

Social media platforms have officially overtaken search engines as a top digital discovery tool, with 49% of global consumers finding new small businesses on social media compared to 40% using search engines.

To capture that audience, entrepreneurs are stepping directly into the role of content creation.

73% of small business owners globally now identify as content creators to some degree.

Within that group, 40% identify primarily as creators and 33% see themselves as an owner/creator hybrid.

Nearly half (47%) of small business owners handle all of their social media management entirely on their own.

AI is helping SMBs get more done faster

Faced with the pressure to act like full-time social media managers – on top of every other task on their plate – entrepreneurs are adopting AI into their daily workflows.

In the US, small business marketing adoption of AI tools has skyrocketed from 26% in 2023 to 87% as of April.

Rather than trying to expand traditional ad budgets to keep pace with larger businesses, 40% of small businesses are leaning on AI and automation specifically to manage their marketing workload.

SMBs aren’t using AI as an experimental hobby; they’re modernizing the way they operate to become more efficient.

50% of AI users globally report that the primary benefit is saving time.

Small business owners are primarily using these tools to write copy and content (42%) and analyze data (38%).

Platform data from Constant Contact shows built-in AI tools reduce campaign and email creation time by up to 23%.

Consumers want to shop small, but budgets are tight

Where customers want to spend their money has shifted dramatically over the last few years. Consumers are actively turning away from giant retailers to spend money at smaller independent brands.

In the US, consumer preference for shopping primarily at small businesses nearly tripled over the last five years, rising from 10% in 2021 to 27% in 2026.

Consumer preference for shopping primarily at large corporations fell from 47% to 33% over the same period.

But due to inflation and rising costs, 49% of US consumers have been forced to scale back their spending at small businesses.

Because consumers have fewer discretionary dollars to go around, they’re being selective about where they shop. A business’s online presence can no longer just look appealing; it has to communicate real value to earn a place in tighter budgets.

How to manage your marketing without burnout

You don’t need a huge budget or an army of employees to capture the wave of consumers who want to spend money with small businesses.

Move #1: Replace polished marketing with authentic storytelling

Consumer preference has evolved: they don’t necessarily want highly produced videos or airbrushed photo shoots; they want something real.

Share the unpolished, behind-the-scenes realities of running your business. Authentic storytelling is often faster and less expensive to produce, and it helps build the kind of human connection that larger businesses struggle to replicate.

Move #2: Treat social media profiles as primary search landing pages

Businesses should treat their social profiles like digital storefronts. Optimize your profiles for people searching for products and services like yours. Treat your bio, captions, and pinned posts like a website homepage. Include relevant keywords, geographic location, operating hours, and product or service descriptions so potential customers can find you.

Move #3: Build your list and send an email

Your email contacts are a list you can own. With tools like Constant Contact, it’s easy to segment your list, set up behavioral triggers, and send the right message at the right time, so you’re working smarter instead of harder.

That ownership is what keeps you off the burnout treadmill. Instead of chasing platform shifts, you get a dependable line to both prospects and existing customers.

Opinions expressed by SmartBrief contributors are their own.

title: Is Sustainable Aviation Fuel Really as Expensive as Headlines Suggest? - ResourceWise
description:

text:
If you read recent headlines about sustainable aviation fuel (SAF), one message seems impossible to escape: SAF is simply too expensive.

Reports from industry stakeholders reveal that costs come down to a several factors:

Billion-dollar compliance costs

Concerns over airline profitability

Warnings that decarbonization could make flying unaffordable

Across the board, the conversation typically paints SAF as an economic burden rather than an opportunity.

But is that really the whole story?

Like many commodity markets, the answer depends on which prices you're looking at and over what timeframe. Temporary supply shortages, policy changes, and market volatility can all distort the perception of what a market truly costs.

For aviation leaders, investors, and fuel suppliers, separating short-term market noise from long-term economics has never been more important. And the difference may paint an altogether different picture of what SAF costs really look like.

Headlines Often Reflect Market Extremes

One of the largest challenges in SAF economics comes down to timing. Many cost estimates are based on today's market conditions rather than tomorrow's.

Commentary from ResourceWise's latest SAF Snapshot highlights several concerns ranging from military fuel budgets to airline operating costs as governments implement SAF mandates and expand carbon pricing. Those concerns are understandable, and new regulations inevitably introduce additional costs into the system.

However, market conditions during the initial rollout of SAF mandates have also been highly unusual.

As the United Kingdom and European Union launched their mandates, buyers entered the market at the same time while available supplies remained relatively limited. The result was a sharp increase in spot pricing as demand temporarily outpaced supply.

This dynamic yields an important set of questions:

Are today's prices representative of the long-term cost of producing SAF?

Or are they simply a reflection of a market adjusting to new demand?

Spot Prices Not the Same as Structural Costs

Many commodity markets experience periods of imbalance regularly:

Oil

Natural gas

Electricity

Renewable diesel

Feedstocks

Sustainable aviation fuel is no different.

During periods of constrained supply, buyers compete aggressively for available product. This pushes prices above long-term production economics.

Those elevated prices may accurately reflect the market today. But they don't necessarily represent where prices will settle as production capacity expands.

This distinction matters because long-term investment decisions are typically based on expected structural production costs and not temporary supply squeezes. Using unusually high spot prices to estimate what SAF will cost in 2035 or 2040 risks overstating the long-term economic challenge.

SAF Market Already Responding to Production Growth

Pricing normalization is expected in the market as higher prices create incentives for additional investment. Around the world, producers are expanding capacity through a growing number of technologies and feedstocks.

The SAF market is no longer limited to traditional HEFA pathways. Investment is accelerating across several areas:

Alcohol-to-Jet (ATJ)

e-Methanol

eSAF

Biomass-derived fuels

Other emerging technologies

All of these solutions aim to improve supply over time. The market is also seeing continued investment in dedicated production facilities across Europe, Africa, Asia, and the Middle East.

As production grows, markets typically become more competitive.

That doesn't necessarily mean SAF will reach price parity with conventional jet fuel overnight. But it does mean today's tight market shouldn't automatically be treated as tomorrow's permanent reality.

The Cost Conversation Must Include Carbon

Another important consideration is what those additional costs actually represent.

Historically, conventional jet fuel has not reflected the environmental cost of its emissions. Carbon pricing and SAF mandates are designed to begin incorporating those external costs into aviation economics. While this increases fuel costs for airlines, it also changes how markets value lower-carbon alternatives.

In other words, the objective isn't simply to make fuel more expensive. It's to create an economic signal that encourages investment in cleaner production pathways while gradually reducing lifecycle emissions.

Viewed through that lens, higher SAF costs are not necessarily evidence that decarbonization is failing. They may simply reflect the market beginning to account for costs that were previously externalized.

Feedstocks Still Drive the Economics

It's also important to remember that SAF pricing doesn't exist in isolation. Feedstocks remain one of the largest determinants of production costs.

SAF pathways are influenced by several different feedstocks and energy sources:

Used cooking oil

Animal fats

Waste ethanol

Vegetable oils

Renewable hydrogen

Electricity

Changes upstream often ripple through the entire value chain, affecting producer margins long before finished fuel prices move. That's why understanding SAF increasingly requires understanding feedstocks.

Related: Feedstock Fundamentals | What are Biofuels Made From?

Markets for waste oils, tallow, renewable power, and alternative fuels often provide earlier signals about future SAF economics than finished fuel prices alone. ResourceWise's market analysis highlights how feedstock movements continue to shape modeled SAF pricing across multiple production pathways.

A Better Question

Instead of asking: "Is SAF too expensive?" industry leaders may be better served asking:

Are current prices driven by structural costs or temporary market conditions?

How quickly is new production capacity coming online?

Which feedstocks are driving economics today?

How will expanding global supply reshape pricing over the next decade?

Those questions move the conversation beyond headlines and toward the underlying market fundamentals.

Looking Beyond Today's Price

The aviation industry's transition to lower-carbon fuels will undoubtedly require investment, policy support, and continued technological innovation. But today's market should not be mistaken for the market of 2035.

As production scales, feedstock markets mature, and new pathways become commercially viable, the economics of sustainable aviation fuel will continue to evolve. For businesses making long-term strategic decisions, understanding those underlying trends (rather than reacting to today's headline prices) will provide a much stronger foundation for navigating the years ahead.

Get a Clear Market Picture with SAF Snapshot Report

The Sustainable Aviation Fuel market is evolving rapidly as new mandates, feedstock dynamics, production technologies, and global trade flows reshape pricing and availability.

ResourceWise’s Monthly SAF Snapshot helps industry participants stay informed on these developments with analyst insights, market commentary, pricing trends, and policy updates from across the global SAF value chain.

Whether you're tracking feedstock markets, monitoring new production capacity, or evaluating emerging regulations, this report provides the context needed to make more informed decisions in an increasingly complex market.

Download the latest edition of the Monthly SAF Snapshot for all the critical updates you need about the fast-moving SAF market.

title: India steps up preparations for sustainable aviation fuel, CORSIA compliance ahead of 2027 ...

During the meeting, officials assessed the status of Sustainable Aviation Fuel production projects being developed by oil marketing companies and reviewed commissioning timelines to ensure adequate fuel availability from 2027 onwards.
Addressing the meeting, Naidu said India views Sustainable Aviation Fuel not merely as a regulatory obligation but as a strategic opportunity to strengthen its aviation ecosystem and contribute to global decarbonisation efforts.
The meeting reviewed the proposed roadmap for SAF blending, including the responsibilities of oil marketing companies, airlines and airport operators.
The minister also informed stakeholders that the draft Sustainable Aviation Fuel policy is in its final stages and is being refined through consultations with various ministries and industry participants.

text:
Union Civil Aviation Minister Ram Mohan Naidu on Wednesday reviewed India’s preparedness for the adoption of Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) and implementation of the Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation (CORSIA), directing all stakeholders to expedite key action points ahead of the mandatory global compliance deadline beginning January 1, 2027.

Chairing a high-level stakeholder meeting organised by the Ministry of Civil Aviation, Naidu reviewed progress in SAF production, certification, supply chain development and the country’s roadmap for meeting future blending requirements under the International Civil Aviation Organization’s (ICAO) global carbon reduction framework.

The meeting was attended by senior officials from the Ministries of Civil Aviation, Petroleum and Natural Gas, and Environment, Forest and Climate Change, along with representatives from the Directorate General of Civil Aviation (DGCA), Airports Authority of India (AAI), Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS), Bureau of Energy Efficiency (BEE), oil marketing companies, airlines, airport operators and other stakeholders.

During the meeting, officials assessed the status of Sustainable Aviation Fuel production projects being developed by oil marketing companies and reviewed commissioning timelines to ensure adequate fuel availability from 2027 onwards. Discussions also focused on certification standards, supply chain development and measures required to support India’s growing aviation sector while reducing carbon emissions.

Addressing the meeting, Naidu said India views Sustainable Aviation Fuel not merely as a regulatory obligation but as a strategic opportunity to strengthen its aviation ecosystem and contribute to global decarbonisation efforts.

“India is committed to building a robust and globally competitive Sustainable Aviation Fuel ecosystem that supports the growth of our aviation sector while contributing meaningfully to global decarbonisation efforts,” the minister said, adding that the SAF value chain would also create opportunities for multiple stakeholders, including farmers.

Highlighting the aviation sector’s progress in sustainability, Naidu said that while no airport operated entirely on green energy in 2014, 104 airports across the country now run on 100 per cent green energy. He added that the government is also encouraging fleet modernisation by promoting aircraft leasing and fuel-efficient aircraft.

The minister stressed the need to move beyond planning and accelerate implementation. He said the government’s immediate priority is to achieve the 1 per cent SAF blending requirement under CORSIA in the most cost-effective manner while simultaneously developing a robust carbon credit offset mechanism through a whole-of-government approach.

The meeting reviewed the proposed roadmap for SAF blending, including the responsibilities of oil marketing companies, airlines and airport operators. Stakeholders also discussed establishing a comprehensive accounting, monitoring and reporting framework aligned with ICAO’s CORSIA requirements, creating a national SAF Registry with end-to-end traceability and facilitating certification and market access.

Naidu said significant progress has already been made in developing the SAF supply chain and carbon accounting systems but directed all concerned agencies to accelerate implementation so that India is fully prepared before the mandatory phase of CORSIA begins in January 2027.

The minister also informed stakeholders that the draft Sustainable Aviation Fuel policy is in its final stages and is being refined through consultations with various ministries and industry participants.

Emphasising that passenger interests remain central to the policy, Naidu said the government aims to ensure that the transition to SAF imposes the least possible financial burden on airlines and travellers by identifying the most cost-effective production, distribution and airport supply mechanisms.

The meeting also reviewed India’s preparedness for CORSIA implementation, including the issuance of Letters of Authorisation and the development of a CORSIA-compliant domestic carbon market framework.

The Ministry reiterated its commitment to expanding domestic Sustainable Aviation Fuel production, reducing emissions from international aviation and positioning India as a global leader in sustainable aviation.

SAF Cost Reduction Pathways Conference

Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) is widely recognised as one of the most effective solutions for reducing carbon emissions from aviation. However, its higher production cost compared with conventional jet fuel remains one of the biggest barriers to large-scale adoption. The SAF Cost Reduction Pathways Conference brings together airlines, fuel producers, technology providers, policymakers, investors, airports, and researchers to explore practical strategies for making SAF more affordable and commercially viable.

A major focus of the conference is improving production efficiency. Experts examine advances in fuel conversion technologies, process optimisation, and next-generation production methods that can increase output while lowering manufacturing costs. Discussions also cover the expansion of sustainable feedstocks, including agricultural residues, forestry waste, municipal solid waste, used cooking oil, and synthetic fuels produced through Power-to-Liquid (PtL) technology.

Investment and financing are another key theme. Building commercial-scale SAF production facilities requires significant capital, and the conference explores innovative funding models, public-private partnerships, and long-term offtake agreements that can provide financial certainty for developers and investors.

Participants also discuss the role of government policies in reducing costs. Blending mandates, tax incentives, grants, carbon pricing mechanisms, and research funding can help create stable market demand and encourage greater investment in SAF production. International collaboration on sustainability standards and certification is also essential for supporting global market growth.

Beyond technical sessions, the conference provides valuable networking opportunities for stakeholders across the aviation fuel value chain. By encouraging collaboration between producers, airlines, airports, financial institutions, and technology companies, the event helps accelerate innovation and strengthen the supply chain needed to scale Sustainable Aviation Fuel.

As the aviation industry works toward its long-term climate goals, reducing the cost of SAF will be critical to increasing production, improving accessibility, and making sustainable air travel a commercial reality.
